memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "Why did you say, 'She is my sister,' so that I took her to be my wife? Now then, here is your wife. Take her and go!" Then Pharaoh gave orders about Abram to his men, and they sent him on his way, with his wife and everything he had. - Gen 12:19-20 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
The chapter ends with Abram being escorted out of Egypt like a criminal. "Take her and go!" A pagan king dismisses the man God had called to bless all nations. Abram leaves with his wealth intact but his testimony in ruins. He came to Egypt for safety and left in disgrace.

Consider what was lost. Abram was meant to be a blessing to all peoples (v.3) - and here, in his first encounter with another nation, he brought them plagues instead of blessing. His witness to Egypt was a lie and a scandal. He had been called to display God's character to the nations and instead displayed cowardice.

Yet notice the mercy woven through it. Abram leaves with his wife. The promise is intact. God's plan is not derailed. Abram walks out shamed but not abandoned, humbled but not cast off.

And here is the good news: this failure is not the end of Abram's story. In the very next chapter, he returns to Bethel - to the altar he had built before - and calls on the name of the Lord again (Gen 13:3-4). Failure is not final for those God has called. If you have stumbled badly, the way back is the way Abram took: return to the altar, call on His name, begin again. God's calling on your life outlasts your worst chapter.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
- Has a failure left you feeling disqualified from God's purposes?
- What would it look like to return to the "altar" and begin again?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text:
Lord, my failures are real, but they are not final in Your hands. Thank You that You do not abandon those You call. Bring me back to the altar, and let me begin again with You.
Amen.
